transcript.text: Gas oven took ages to light tonight then went WHOOMPH and now the kitchen smells really strongly of gas even though I've turned it off. Is it safe to try again?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
If you can smell gas, treat it as an emergency: don't turn any switches on or off and no naked flames. Turn the gas off at the meter if you safely can, open doors and windows, and leave if the smell is strong. Call the National Gas Emergency line on 0800 111 999.

oh god ok. the meter is in a box outside by the front door, should I go turn it off there? the smell is still really strong and I've got a slight headache. I'm renting so can't reach my landlord tonight

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Then move away from the property into fresh air. Because the smell is still very strong and you have a headache, call the National Gas Emergency line now on 0800 111 999 from outside or a neighbour’s phone. Do not try the oven again or go back in to investigate it. If you feel faint, confused, very unwell, or the headache is worsening, call 999. The delayed lighting followed by a whoomph suggests unburnt gas built up before ignition; it could be an ignition or gas-control fault, but it must be made safe and checked by a Gas Safe engineer before the cooker is used again. Your landlord can deal with the repair afterwards; the emergency gas response comes first.

reading.symptom: Took ages to light, then ignited with a WHOOMPH; strong gas smell remains after turning it off

candidates: Gas escaping after delayed ignition, possibly from the oven ignition or gas-control system (high)
plan: They asked: "Should I turn the gas off at the outside meter?" - answer that first.

Safety: they reported a gas smell earlier and were given the emergency advice. Do not repeat it. Do not suggest any check or use of the appliance; answer what they ask now, and make sure they know to keep following that advice until a Gas Safe engineer has made it safe.

The fault they reported is: "Took ages to light, then ignited with a WHOOMPH; strong gas smell remains after turning it off". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
